story|title:i tried every llm architectu.content_excerpt: The best architecture change since GPT-3 is fine-grained MoE, linear attention and hyper-connections work. Architecture research is one of the highest aura jobs you can have right now. Open a tech report and architecture gets a huge chunk of it. There's also this mystery around it, like all this stuff was invented by some gigabrains who look at raw tensor printouts, see the norm blowups, and come up with manifold-constrained hyperconnectors or whatever. There are also opinions that architecture probably isn't that important. That the data and proper pre-training (and especially post-training) setup tuning is where the big wins are. All the rumors that frontier labs are training the most boring transformers ever, that "pre-training is dead", and all this "old data, modern arch vs modern data, old arch" discourse. I wanted to put the architecture decisions that open labs and researchers made over the last six years into the same setup and see which ones held up. So I ran more than 1,000 experiments, trying the changes on their own and then stacking the winners to see how much of the improvement survived. I'd been thinking about this "mega-ablation" for over a year. Coding agents finally made it doable in a reasonable amount of time. I trained all these weird models with bux , the framework I built for architecture experiments. You can define an architecture, train it, export it to vLLM, and measure both quality and inference speed. I trained on a mix of code files and whole Python repositories from Stack-Edu, plus web text from FineWeb-Edu, using AdamW. Training starts with 2k-token sequences and ends with a 16k context extension. The recipe: Each architecture gets a short learning-rate sweep: 1e-3, 2e-3 and 4e-3 at d = 512 d=512 d = 512 , plus 8e-3 for changes that claim to help stability. I fit a parabola in log learning rate and reuse its minimum at the wider models. I measure quality in bits per byte (BPB) on held-out data: 0.5 × code files + 0.3 × whole repositories + 0.2 × web text. Repositories are read in 16k-token windows, so long context counts. Lower is better: -2% means 2% fewer bits per byte. Changing only the seed moves the objective by about 0.7%. Runs with the same seed see the same data in the same order, so we always compare runs that share a seed. That cuts the noise of a comparison to about 0.3%. story|title:my agent org speedran a comp.content_excerpt: Last week, from November 2 to 8, our engineering organization merged 1,119 pull requests into Perfloop, pushing the repository past 39,000 commits on main since April. That is the weekly throughput of a very large software company, except every engineer in the org is a coding agent running on Amp, and I run the whole company through a single chat thread. What nobody tells you before you run a fleet of agents at that scale is that when you tell them to organize themselves like an engineering company, they don't just ship code like a big company. They build the bureaucracy of one too. Given three weeks and a git repository, my agents invented an executive layer, review committees, 386 numbered compliance grants and watcher threads whose only job was to watch other watcher threads, and grew their rulebook to 277,486 characters. Then came the part no human company has ever pulled off. When I asked the coordinating agent I had made VP of Engineering why three alerts had been firing for two days while status reports stayed green, it audited the entire bureaucracy it had built, assigned blame for every rule, handed off its work, and fired itself in 47 minutes. Three weeks later, the rebuilt org was shipping at twice its old peak. If 1,119 pull requests a week sounds like an impossible amount of code to review, it is. At 160 pull requests a day, human code review is a polite fiction. Even at a tenth of that pace, coding agents produce diffs way faster than any team has the attention to read closely. The test suite stays green, the diff looks clean on GitHub, and buried three calls deep is a hot path allocating ten times the memory it used to, an edge case returning the wrong answer, or an untrusted input nobody had a spare afternoon to trace. That is the wall every team hits once coding agents take off, and it is why we built Perfloop. Agents write the code. Perfloop keeps it fast, right and safe. Point it at a repository and it works in the background all day, hunting for those quiet problems and proving every patch inside a sandbox before a person ever sees a pull request. Since June, outside maintainers have merged 120 of Perfloop's changes across 30 projects (including Prometheus® , ClickHouse , Redis , PostgreSQL and the Go runtime ), and every one of them improved code that had already passed review.
